title: No controversy over whether free choice exists: the Reformed hold it survives the fall, weakened and enslaved
source_text: I. Thesibus superioribus breviter & dilucide, quantum in nobis fuit, exposuimus doctrinam de Libero hominis arbitrio absolute & in se spectato, primo juxta Scholae Reformatae Doctores, deinde juxta mentem Doctorum Scholae Romanae. Ac ante omnia manifestum fecimus nullam esse controversiam de Libero hominis arbitrio circa quaestionem, An sit. Quandoquidem Reformati omnes fatentur non solum hominem, quum primum a Deo conditus est, praeditum fuisse libero arbitrio; sed etiam in homine lapso idem liberum arbitrium mansisse, nec in eo prorsus extinctum & amissum fuisse; quanquam per lapsum hominis valde infirmatum fuerit, & in servitutem peccati redactum, donec per Christi gratiam in libertatem asseratur.
pass_a_gloss: In the preceding Theses we have set forth briefly and clearly, as far as lay in us, the doctrine of the free choice of man considered absolutely and in itself, first according to the Doctors of the Reformed School, then according to the mind of the Doctors of the Roman School. And before all things we made it manifest that there is no controversy about the free choice of man concerning the question, Whether it be. Since all the Reformed confess not only that man, when he was first created by God, was endowed with free choice; but also that in fallen man the same free choice has remained, and has not been altogether extinguished and lost in him; although through man's fall it has been greatly weakened, and reduced into the bondage of sin, until it be set into liberty through the grace of Christ.
pass_b_english: The foregoing theses have set out, as briefly and clearly as we could, the doctrine of man's free choice taken absolutely and in itself: first as the teachers of the Reformed School hold it, then as the teachers of the Roman School understand it.

Above all, they showed that there is no dispute over whether man has free choice at all. Every Reformed theologian grants that man was given free choice when God first made him, and that the same free choice survived in man after the fall and was not wholly destroyed or lost. The fall badly weakened it and brought it into slavery to sin, until Christ's grace sets it free.

lemmas.gloss: reduced into the bondage of sin

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
